analysis.one_liner: Bans housing discrimination against people who pay rent with vouchers, benefits, or child support.
analysis.headline: The Fair Housing Improvement Act of 2022 never received a committee vote or floor action and died when Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added three new protected classes to the Fair Housing Act: source of income, veteran status, and military status. Landlords, sellers, real estate brokers, and lenders could no longer refuse to deal with someone because their money comes from a housing voucher, Social Security, a disability benefit, child support, or any other lawful source. Today a landlord can legally turn away a veteran or a voucher holder simply because of how they pay; this bill would have made that a civil rights violation nationwide.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and homebuyers whose income is legal but non-traditional: families using Section 8 housing vouchers, people on Social Security or disability benefits, recipients of child support or spousal support, veterans, and active-duty service members. In many states, none of these protections exist today, so a landlord can decline a complete application for no reason other than the source of the money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voucher holders, benefit recipients, veterans, military families

how_it_helps.text: Adds source of income, veteran status, and military status as protected classes under the Fair Housing Act, covering the rental, sale, and financing of housing.

Defines source of income to include Section 8 vouchers, all federal, state, and local housing assistance, Social Security and SSI benefits, Railroad Retirement benefits, court-ordered child and spousal support, payments from trusts or relatives, and savings.

Extends the federal criminal provision against intimidation and interference in housing rights to cover these new protected classes, so threatening someone over a voucher or their veteran status would be a federal offense.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords, rental property owners, and some real estate and mortgage professionals, who would face new anti-discrimination obligations and possible legal liability. Some property owners argue that renting to voucher holders brings extra paperwork, inspections, and payment timing issues, and that this rule would leave them no lawful way to screen those tenants out.

drawbacks.text: The bill would compel housing providers to accept tenants whose income comes partly from government agencies, which can involve unit inspections, additional documentation, and payments that arrive on a different schedule than a private paycheck. Small landlords who do not want that administrative burden would lose the option of screening for it.

It creates a new federal standard on top of a patchwork of state and local source-of-income laws, and covered landlords and housing agencies would need to adjust their practices and train staff to comply nationwide.

The bill also extends, for up to 40 months (plus a possible 6-month extension in exceptional cases), the period during which existing state and local fair housing agencies are deemed certified, a grace period that delays stricter federal recertification of those agencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and targeted: it removes a lawful way to refuse housing to voucher holders, benefit recipients, and veterans, groups that today can be rejected for reasons unrelated to their ability to pay rent. The main cost falls on housing providers in the form of compliance and, for some, the loss of a screening tool they preferred. The main design criticism is not the goal but the burden-shifting: the bill mandates acceptance without adding resources to smooth the payment and inspection frictions that make some landlords reluctant to participate in voucher programs. On balance, the protections address a real civil rights gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee in November 2022, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters introduced the bill on June 23, 2022, with four colleagues, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties.
No further action was taken; the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners who prefer not to rent to voucher holders or benefit recipients are better off, because the rule they would have had to follow was never enacted. Renters relying on those income sources are in the same legal position as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords who screen out voucher holders

for.name: Rep. Scott Peters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Housing Improvement Act of 2022 in the House.

for.name: 11 of 222 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 12 Democratic backers in the House and none from the other party.

against.name: Rep. Jerry Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing; after the initial referral the bill was sent to a subcommittee and no further action followed.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; because the bill never advanced, no vote was ever taken and no opposition was ever recorded on the record.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from refusing tenants because their income comes from vouchers, benefits, or child support, and would create legal liability for doing so. That screening practice is how some owners keep voucher participants out, so the bill's gain is exactly where the public's gain sits: on the other side of that practice.

industries.industry: Real estate brokers and mortgage lenders
industries.note: Sections covering brokerage and lending would also prohibit discrimination based on these new classes, adding compliance duties for professionals who steer or finance housing transactions, while expanding the pool of clients they may lawfully serve.

industries.industry: State and local fair housing agencies
industries.note: These agencies enforce fair housing law and would take on three new protected classes, while the bill extends their federal certification window by up to 40 months to adjust.
